We saw a small (approximately 5 miles in diameter); isolated; green cell that was southeast of our position on the radar depiction. Nothing worse than light and occasional moderate turbulence was experienced. ATC advised us that arriving aircraft had only reported light to moderate turbulence. We continued to stay on right deviations to clear the small isolated green cell just out of caution. I tilted my radar down to confirm the cell was painting correctly on the radar (approximately -0.5 to get the clearest reading without ground clutter at approximately 25 nm) and advised the FO that we should be able to turn direct the KLEET after the flight path showed south of the cell. At this point; the FO had his radar tilted up at approximately +2.0. I told the FO to reduce the tilt in order to view the light precipitation cell. We proceeded direct to KLEET after the dashed direct to line showed us well clear of the small cell. There was no depiction of any precip on our flight path direct to KLEET. The small isolated green cell was at least 10 nm north of our position. Current conditions were IMC but no visible precipitation and no more visible lightning; occasional light to moderate chop. After a few minutes of turning direct to KLEET we experienced severe turbulence. The airspeed became erratic by rapidly decreasing and trending a large decrease. The plane violently began to climb (approximately 100-200 ft) then rapidly descend. The FO took manual control of the throttles trying best to maintain M0.76. The aircraft was unable to maintain altitude and became stable at 32;600 FT. The FO began the climb back to FL330 and I advised ATC that we experienced severe turbulence. I immediately called the flight attendants to insure there were no injuries. I advised ATC that there were no injuries; no aircraft damage and no precip at the time of the severe turbulence. We continued the flight to MIA since there were no injuries or noticeable damage to the aircraft.Cause: Severe weather over Florida and an unexpected arrival change into MIA.It may have been a more conservative option to stay on the full arrival and not accept a clearance direct to KLEET. However; other aircraft were ahead of us on the arrival and there was no indication of threats/turbulence/precip going direct to KLEET.

Flight left as normal; preflight was normal. On climb right engine fluctuations to maximum 77%. Continued climb to 9000 ft. Around 200 ft short 2450 RPMs gave an indication of HI RH MAP CAS (Crew Alert System) message. We leveled off and set cruise power. All indications were normal when about 20 mins in flight we started losing power on RH engine. 2100 RPM's were producing maximum 57% with full throttle and upon increasing RPMs to 2200; the power output was 67%. Considering a high-density altitude; and a hot day we decided to turn back to ZZZ for the safety of flight.

During preflight review of aircraft status; aircraft was noted to have a deferred APU. Gate Preconditioned Air (PCA) was connected at the time; and was not satisfactory to cool down the cabin prior to boarding. Once an external air cart was connected to the aircraft for engine start purposes; the Captain and I elected to run both packs to cool down the cabin. Almost immediately I noticed an exhaust smell; which I believed was simply fumes ingested from the ramp area. As the cabin was cooling down; Maintenance was onboard resolving a pressurization controller issue. Once Maintenance work was completed; the Captain also noticed the smell and we both decided to shut down the packs until necessary to cool down the cabin with PAX on board. Approximately 2-3 minutes after turning off the packs; the cockpit began filling with visible smoke. The Captain; Maintenance personal; and I all investigated and could not determine the source. Maintenance inspected the Electronic Equipment (E/E) Compartment with no trace of the smoke. Captain then refused the airplane; and we deplaned the aircraft without further incident. We both visited the onsite clinic and removed ourselves from duty for the rest of the day.Cause: This issue couldn't have been mitigated by ensuring the APU was operating; especially during summer months in ZZZ.'
Narrative 2 - 'Was in preflight preparing for our flight to ZZZ1. The APU was deferred and crew ran the packs off the air start cart for approximately 20 minutes. We had an Estimated Departure Clearance Time (EDCT) so we shut down the packs and were using only preconditioned air to cool the aircraft for the 10 minutes prior to the event. At the same time we found an issue with the pressurization control panel and called ZZZ Maintenance. A maintenance technician arrived and resolved the pressurization panel issue. As he was getting ready to leave the Captain; First Officer (FO); and AMT noticed smoke of unknown origin in the flight deck. No smoke was noticed in the passenger cabin. The maintenance technician checked the Electrical Equipment (E and E) compartment for any indication of the origin of the smoke but found none.A maintenance supervisor was called and on his arrival the Captain refused the aircraft on the basis of smoke of unknown origin. The crew left the aircraft; the cockpit crew removed themselves from any further flying this day and reported to the medical clinic at ZZZ for evaluation. Examination by the doctor on duty showed both the Captain and First Officer fit for duty and both deadheaded to their home bases that evening.Cause: Possible issues with either the air-start cart; the air conditioning packs; or Preconditioned Air (PCA).

After takeoff and climbing IFR to cleared 11;000 ft. on heading 295 ex ZZZ Runway XX into gusty conditions and moderate turbulence 'GPWS/ WIND SHEAR FAIL' was displayed on both Primary Flight Displays (PFDs). Then 'X' displayed on both PFD HSIs in FMS mode.I glanced at the FMS Control Display Unit (CDU) just in time to see it flash a white screen and then go blank. PFDs and Multifunction Flight Displays (MFDs) then blanked. I communicated to ATC that we had a navigation issue; took controls and started to level off the aircraft from climb at approximately 10;000 ft. I requested the First Officer (FO) to advise that we were having nav/ instrument issues.At the time of the failures Autopilot remained engaged. Remainder of flight was made with Autopilot off and on standby instruments. I checked the voltage indicator and it looked normal/ straight up/ above 24V. I selected battery to EMERGENCY to conserve battery power as we were descending in IFR. ATC gave descent to 2;000 ft. and vectors to approach XX .When we were visual and could continue visual to Runway XX I selected battery back to ON. Normal configuration and landing made back to ZZZ. At some point during descent and positioning for approach all displays and FMS returned to displaying information. FMS was initializing. My attention was solely focused on a safe return and landing while flying IFR on STANDBY Instruments. I'm not exactly sure when the FMS and displays returned however I am pretty sure that they returned while the battery was selected to EMER which was confusing and why I recall it as such.Landing ZZZ was approximately 540 pounds overweight

Received an ACARS message at XA:09:15 that said R ENG SHUTDOWN RETURN TO ZZZ2. Priority handling was requested; Crash Fire Rescue rolled trucks. Aircraft taxied to gate. Did a tail swap and crew was good with continuing. Crew spoke with operations and said when climbing through 17;000 ft.; they had an oil pressure caution and the oil pressure dropped to zero. Crew ran the QRH and shutdown the right engine and returned to ZZZ2. Not much we can do to prevent this from happening in the future.

After exiting the runway we started APU. There was a delay in gate assignment due to congestion in ZZZ. Shortly after a normal APU start; the FA2 (Flight Attendant) heard a loud 'pop' followed by oily odor in the aft part of the cabin. The FA1 alerted the flight crew of the smell in the cabin. The EICAS filled up with messages. We shut down the APU and the odor cleared immediately although the EICAS messages all remained. Shortly thereafter our gate opened up and we taxied in uneventfully. Maintenance was notified.

Aircraft X ZZZ to ZZZ1. On the beginning of a three-day pairing; during the walk around; the FO (First Officer) found possible evidence of a bird strike in the #2 Engine. ZZZ Maintenance was called out and inspected the aircraft for a bird strike. The inspection was written up and the logbook was cleared in accordance with the maintenance manual. No damage found and Maintenance said the aircraft was good to go; so we departed for ZZZ1 only eight minutes late and landed uneventfully. Upon our arrival Maintenance put a lock on the aircraft for an incomplete inspection. ZZZ1 Maintenance completed the inspection in the first 30 minutes of our ground time. Maintenance took the aircraft out of service two hours later because they could not get the new Maintenance Software Program to accept the write-up and took the aircraft out of service.

Flying the NAPAA4.NAPAA departure out of APC airport we loaded the departure into the FMS and verified the routing was correct.As we departed the airport on Runway 19R with a clearance to climb to 3;000 feet we had the autopilot engaged in LNAV and vertical speed. Autothrottles where set at 200 kts.As we started our climb there was a piston single that had departed Runway 19L ahead of us. As we climbed out I had the other aircraft in sight but did get a traffic alert on the TCAS. I think at the time we received the TCAS alert he was already passing off our left wing and 400 feet below us. The autopilot made an initial slight right turn towards the VOR and then sequenced the next leg of our flight plan from the SGD VOR to SAC as was filed on our flight plan.Due to the tight turn that would be required to fly the leg from SGD to SAC I thought it had initiated the turn early in anticipation of our proximity to the VOR and that we were approaching our assigned altitude of 3;000 feet.Between the TCAS alert and seeing that the FMS was sequenced now to fly to the next fix on our flight plan I was focused on ensuring we maintained our separation from the other aircraft and after verifying that the FMS was sequenced to our cleared route I continued in the left turn and established the aircraft on the leg from SGD to SAC.Tower handed us off to Oakland [Center] and it was then that they inquired as to why we had made a left turn after takeoff rather than flying the departure as published. We had a brief exchange with the Controller about how the FMS had sequenced us on the next leg of the flight plan prior to reaching the VOR.Upon landing at our final destination later in the day I placed a call to Oakland Center as well as the Tower at APC. The Oakland Controller that I spoke with did not think there had been any issue with what happened since we had not been given a phone number to call from our Controller. When I called the Tower at APC; I was able to speak with the controller that cleared us for takeoff and handed us off to Oakland when we departed. He stated that they have had a few aircraft making the same left turn after takeoff while flying that same departure. He indicated that they needed to look into it and said that there had not been any conflict with other traffic. He thanked me for getting back to him and talking to him about it and that he would be following up the next day with his colleagues regarding this departure.Our filed and cleared route was APC NAPAA4 SGD SAC ZZZ ZZZ1.

I was pilot monitoring. We were given a clearance to maintain 250 knots until advised. Upon reaching 10;000 feet we accelerated to 290 knots (our normal profile). I advised the Captain that we were given a 250 knot clearance...we discussed and I probed the Controller and confirmed we were given a 250 knot speed restriction until 14;000 feet. We began to slow down. I believe the cause of this is the fact that we have not been flying a lot because of COVID. I had been furloughed and brought back to the line and retrained. I believe if I had been flying more often than I would have been able to catch this lapse earlier or could have reminded the Captain once we reached 10;000 feet.

Inadvertently pushed back without final DG report. Threats included late arrival at airport due to traffic and hurricane. We arrived at the aircraft 35 minutes prior to push. Since we were time compressed; I set up the cockpit while the First Officer (FO) did the walk around which is not our normal flow. During initialization I received a planned DG report indicating dry ice. I printed the report and placed it between the thrust levers as a reminder to myself; due to distractions (briefing the purser; speaking to gate agent; etc.) I failed to mention the planned DG to the FO. When all doors were closed; purser indicated cabin ready and headset operator indicating he was ready to push we completed the before push checklist and i released the parking brake and told the headset operator brakes released; standby" after we got pushback clearance from ground control and commenced pushback I realized we had neither final weights or final DG report. I queried the headset operator and he told me the ramp was in the process of closing out the flight. I also called operations and was advised that due to the weather the ramp was running late. We completed the pushback and we did not start engines until we received the final DG report and sent the code. I should have briefed the FO on the planned DG but I allowed myself to get distracted. I will redouble my efforts to make sure that does not occur again."

On the departure ATC cleared us to climb to 10000 feet; we were vectored to avoid a very powerful cell that was in the path of the departure when we were close to level 10000 we were assigned to climb via; the SID witch has a top altitude of 12000; before reaching ZZZZZ intersection we were hit by moderate to severe turbulence with altitude gains of 2000ft and loss of 1000ft. At that point the automatic pilot struggled to keep the published altitude and we got really busy handling the situation; we managed to return to 10000ft but the publish altitude was busted. ATC notified us about a possible deviation and a phone number was given

I was selected for a random screening upon arrival at the airport. I was given a very thorough and time-consuming search; and thus arrived at the aircraft about 20 minutes prior to pushback. The First Officer had to do all of the preflight prep in my absence. We were unable to get the takeoff data message and after some troubleshooting realized we had missed an incorrect flight number that was loaded in the FMC. It was some combination of 1 and 0; which is probably why we missed it; but not the correct [number]. After correcting this error we were able to get the takeoff message. Upon brake release; we immediately received a notification form warning. I queried the Tug Operator if they had loaded dangerous goods (DG) and he replied yes; so we sent a dangerous goods summary request and subsequently acknowledged the dangerous goods; dry ice.Technically we had released the brakes prior to acknowledging the DG; which is not in accordance with SOP. We did not push without the acknowledgment. The notification form warning states prior to aircraft movement; while the DG summary states prior to brake release; which is more conservative.

On departure from ZZZ; ED2 displayed many temporary messages and I noticed an intermittent FMS flag on PFD1. The FO (First Officer) reported a burnt plastic smell; and GEN 1 went offline with a GEN1 caution message.  Since the APU was deferred; we were single gen.  We requested our present heading and a level off altitude; which ATC gave us.  We complied with the QRH for GEN1 caution; and the message did not clear.  We requested priority handling.  We messaged Dispatch that we wanted to return ZZZ; Dispatch agreed; and we requested delay vectors to burn off fuel.  L window; and L windshield caution messages were still posted from the initial round of messages.  We completed the QRH for L windshield and the messages cleared.  We requested landing on XXC and said we would advise approach when we were ready.  We talked to the FA (Flight Attendant); then briefed the passengers; saying we would be returning to ZZZ as a precaution; we would be on the ground in about 40 minutes; airport equipment might be standing by as a precaution; and we expected a normal landing.  We prepared for the approach; accomplished all checklists and returned to ZZZ.  We landed below max landing weight.  ARFF was standing by; so we requested they inspect the left engine.  They reported no smoke or leaking so we requested taxi to the gate.  I asked the crew if they were okay; they said yes.  No passengers reported being distressed.We decided since there was no apparent indication that there was a fire to decline ARFF (Airport Rescue Fire Fighting) services initially.  Perhaps we should have requested them regardless.  Based on recommendations of our previous [supervisor]; we decided to request priority handling as a precaution.  The benefits of priority handling seemed necessary for us in the event the situation deteriorated.  This is also why I requested Runway XXC.  It was the closest runway for the airport's configuration at the time.  My thinking was that if a fire started; we should be prepared for the approach which would minimize the distance traveled as well as the aircraft that might need to be vectored out of our way.  It also made sense to me to use a runway that was already in use if we did not require special handling.  Those were the things I saw as risk factors for landing after an inflight fire.  We also considered some of the airports below us as we received delay vectors.  I am open to suggestions from the [Review Team] about how I might improve my decision-making skills as it relates to this scenario.

I began my preflight; engine cowling inspection; along with all calculations needed prior to my flight.  I began to taxi to runway XX. The winds were at 050 and 10 kts when I listened before taking off. I never heard the station broadcast system say the gust factor prior to or while in flight. I then began my take off and climbed up to pattern altitude. A PC-12 was coming in on a 8 mile base leg from the south for runway XY. I made my crosswind pattern leg and departed to the south maintained visual separation and let the PC-12 know I was not a factor. I then waited until they landed and said clear of the runway XY to begin a re-entry to the pattern on the downwind leg for runway XY via a 45° entry. I then did all procedures in the pattern needed; and came in for a touch and go on runway XY. Had no issues on approach; landing or takeoff; I then did another lap in the pattern following all procedures needed. Once I was on final my approach was stable I hit a pocket of very slight turbulence but maintained a  stable approach. I then landed; did all procedures to begin takeoff and then began to rotate; after reaching rotation speed. At lift off I felt either turbulence or a gust of wind dictate the plane causing the plane to dance around and since I was low to the ground I tried to not let the plane get off course or any unusual attitude. Then once I was at a safe altitude in the pattern; Aircraft Y had told me the winds changed and were now favoring runway XZ. I then departed the traffic pattern again on the crosswind leg to the south and listened in to the weather station. Which did state the winds were at 330. So I waited for Aircraft Y to depart from the pattern and began to rejoin the traffic pattern again on the downwind leg at a 45° entry but for runway XZ. I did all of the procedures needed for the pattern. Once I was on final; I had a stable approach and landed safely on XZ and began to taxi back to parking. I then checked the tanks for remaining fuel and oil levels after engine shut off the aircraft parked and tied down. I did not notice any damage to the aircraft while checking the tanks or engine.

On my return flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 over [freeway]; I descended below 1000 ft. AGL and at a point below 500 ft. from the highest obstacle because of changing terrain elevation. I did not realize there were houses on the hills. I do not feel that I put anyone in jeopardy and I had a plan for an emergency landing that minimized risk to other civilians and myself. However; trying to avoid the Bravo; I descended too quickly down the descending terrain from ZZZ into the ZZZ1. I was unfamiliar with this route as I usually travel more easterly. My GPS alerted me of terrain at 500 ft AGL; I quickly leveled off and the terrain continued to descend which put me back into the correct altitude. I am now aware of the terrain limitations and more comfortable with this route.

Aircraft X arrived as flight from ZZZ. The flight crew reported the right Nose cowl anti-ice valve illuminated in flight. Company Maintenance Control was notified and the decision to place it on Mel 30-00-XX-X; with associated Mel 36-00-XX. The AMM references were received and the right engine was opened to lock the nose cowl anti ice valve in the open position and the high stage valve in the closed position. The AMM calls for the cannon plug to the TAI (Thermal Anti Ice) pressure switch to be disconnected. While in the process of completing the MEL procedure I was receiving maintenance call from our other business partners. I disconnected the cannon plug for the anti ice valve instead of the pressure switch. The high stage valve was locked closed and engine cowls closed. The log book signed and aircraft released for service. The aircraft left the gate and returned to gate after EICAS warning. Upon arrival back to gate the right engine fan cowl was opened. The anti ice valve cannon plug reconnected and the TAI pressure switch cannon plug disconnected per the AMM. The engine fan cowl was closed and the logbook signed. The root cause for this incident was the distraction of the incoming maintenance calls and not going back three steps to make sure the proper cannon plug was disconnected. The aircraft left the gate and the fight arrived to ZZZ without further problems.

On Date; I flew Aircraft X to ZZZ1 for my instrument check ride which was scheduled for XA AM on Date1.After my check ride I flew VFR back to ZZZ from ZZZ1. Conditions were VFR for the entire route. The weather at ZZZ1 was hot and humid and winds were extremely gusty out of the southwest when I departed. I had a great tailwind and a very bumpy but uneventful quick trip back.ZZZ ATIS revealed the winds were increasing at ZZZ. I believe the wind was reported 220 at around 16 kts or so. TRACON told me to expect Runway XX.I flew a normal VFR right downwind pattern to Runway XX. Everything was fine. On final; I did a wind-check and I recall the winds were increasing and were 220 or 230 at over 20 kts. I opted for two notches of flaps instead of 3 due to the gusty and crosswind conditions. I was on glide-slope according to the PAPI.On short final I was centered up well; had a crosswind correction in and had the nose lined up with the runway. I landed the airplane and got all the wheels on the ground. Just moments after; I apparently got a very strong gust from the left on roll out. The airplane went hard right at a significant enough angle where it was impossible for me not to go on the grass. I was able to recover a bit and just left the edge of the runway; but enough to strike one runway light. I got the airplane slowed down and turned left on Taxiway XX.Following that; the plane taxied and sounded fine. There was apparently no damage to the nose-wheel or propeller as I noticed nothing different about the performance of the plane on taxi.I believe I maintained my crosswind correction during rollout but I am certainly open to the possibility that I did not; or had an inadequate crosswind correction for the strength of the gusty crosswind I experienced. I; of course; was the PIC (Pilot in Command) and take full responsibility.I notified Tower immediately during taxi. They offered assistance but I did not require any. I fueled the plane; cleaned it up and put it in its hanger. I then called and notified my Instructor who made sure the airplane was taken out of service. I attempted to call Tower but discovered I did not have their number. I talked to the Supervisor at Tower the next morning.In my less than 5 years of being a pilot. About 75% of my hours are in a 172. The balance of my hours are in my Cherokee 6 and Aircraft Y During my instrument training; I have logged about 50 hours in Aircraft X in 2.5 months.Without question; I have never experienced anything close to what occurred on Date1. I have certainly landed in similar or worse conditions. But could I have done anything differently? Yes. Perhaps use on one notch of flaps or none. Or I could have had more of a crosswind correction on rollout. Again; I'm not sure how much I used during landing. I also could've not landed at ZZZ if I felt that I couldn't land the plane safely. I could've landed at ZZZ2 on Runway XY with less crosswind.I'll certainly always have this experience in my mind when I fly in the future. I'm quite humble when it comes to flying and I have conservative personal minimums. I know there is always room for improvement. And that a good pilot is always learning.**Just a side note. A few days after the incident with my Instructor for 3 hours. We spent a lot of time doing soft field/short field takeoff and landings in a very significant crosswind.

Everything was normal and we were holding short of RWY4 at the ILS critical line. Tower cleared us into position and hold and said be ready to go traffic four miles out. As soon as we were lined up we were cleared for takeoff with a heading that differed from our original clearance. The takeoff roll was normal with normal callouts. At rotation I realized something was wrong with my flight guidance and FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator). It was in pink ALT and airspeed was FMS 210. Once I confirmed we had power and airspeed I pitched up to a normal climb attitude and we fixed the FMA to what was needed. While this was happening we entered wake turbulence from the preceding A220 that took off. During cruise we tried to determine what happened and we couldn't figure out what we did wrong. FO said he noticed something was off during the initial takeoff roll. Suggestions: Not sure of what happened so I don't know.'
Narrative 2 - 'Flight went normal up until we received our takeoff clearance. We were told to hold short of the ILS critical area for Runway 4 by Ground. As we came to a stop; Tower cleared us to line up and wait expect no delay traffic on a 4 mile final". As we turned to line up with the runway we were given a no delay takeoff clearance; as well as fly heading 020. (We were cleared the Bronx climb) Power was set; engines were spooled; and I called TOGA set. Something caught my eye though. Around 40ish knots I saw our speed was listed as 210 and pink. My initial thought was it must be in manual mode on accident. I realized it was pink; and instinctively moved my hand towards the MCDU (Multipurpose Control Display Unit) to check the speeds; but recognized the takeoff roll is not the time to be doing anything like that. I went back to a scan and saw that our flight director wanted a slight turn to the left; even though we were perfectly down the center of the runway. We passed though 80 knots and all had felt and looked normal outside. I called v1 and rotate; but the flight director didn't respond much. It kept a slight turn and a nose low attitude. At this point we realized something was not right. We called heading and VNAV as normal and hand flew the airplane. While going into VNAV I realized that the FMA was somehow in ALT mode. Once we changed to heading and FLCH; the flight director returned to normal. Suggestions: We don't know what happened or how it happened. We tried thoroughly talking through what we saw and when but couldn't pinpoint the "what or where" we went wrong. For me though as an FO looking back; I should have called for an abort. I was still In "what's wrong" mode instead of "something is not right; let's abort and get reconfigured" mode. Calling an abort is easy if something big happens like an engine failure. But in that moment passing though that 60 to 80 knot range we were still in a low speed abort regime; and I wish I would have called for it. My thought should have been to abort instead of thinking to check the speeds on the MCDU. That thought did not cross my mind until around Vr and at that point we were committed."

As we were about to start the approach ATC gave us a vector towards terrain for spacing.  We immediately said this was not right we stopped our descent and requested a right turn back to the IAF to avoid terrain. The approach was completed without incident.

I landed on Runway 3. The surface was black ice with braking action nil. I departed the runway off the right edge. The airplane came to an immediate stop upon contact with snowy terrain. Actions prior to the incident including checking NOTAMs for anything regarding runway conditions and texting the Airport Manager for field conditions. There were no NOTAMS and the Airport Manager did not reply. I looked over the runway and saw no snow on the surface and could see all of the black color of the asphalt. I landed normally. The aircraft began slowing with brake application but when I got down to about 10 to 20 kts. I began sliding until the plane came to a stop.The airplane was not damaged and was easily recovered from the grass. After inspection; it was returned to service.What could have prevented this would be a proactive approach to reporting runway conditions. The airport operator could have posted a NOTAM about poor to nil braking action. He observed wet runways at close of business the day before and the temperature was forecasted to be well below freezing.  A NOTAM would have been good; or an advisory when contacted directly would been useful. Armed with better information; I could have diverted to an alternate.

The Captain informed the flight attendants about a potential tail tip when we got to our gate. He stated we would leave seatbelt sign on and passengers seated while ground crew unloaded bags to help with the tail tip situation. The seatbelt sign stayed on and the doors were still armed. FA A (Flight Attendant) noticed the gate agent moving the jet bridge to door 1L. She said he did 2 knocks and didn't even check for thumbs up. She was on the other side indicating a no motion with her hands; telling him not to open. He started to open the door so she pushed down on the door operating handle while FA B; quickly disarmed door. There was no slide deployment but we informed gate agent he needed to wait for the thumbs up. We were flying the Airbus and there is a safety guard so it is supposed to disarm from the outside; but proper procedures we have in place to ensure no ISDs (Inadvertent Slide Deployments) are caused was not followed by the gate agent. Captain then turned the seatbelt sign off and  Flight Attendant B made disarming announcement. I then disarmed my door (1R) and had Flight Attendant B cross check my door; but as hers was already opened I couldn't complete the proper cross check to her door. We informed captain about the situation.

[Company] Leadership for years under hydration program created several locations housing ice makers; ice merchandisers; filtered water dispensers and water cooler sanitizing station.Yesterday [the gate] crew was seriously upset as aircraft maintenance team was working on [an aircraft] to clear clogged sewer line in aft; once maintenance team was done they walked to the sanitizing station at [an adjacent gate] meant for washing only drinking water coolers to wash their used tools. Even before [the] team could actually approach and prevent the act the maintenance team had already started the unbelievable act.Maintenance washed their dirty sewer tools and left. The act was reported to Supervisor on duty who reported to [operations] and Manager on duty about the act; who suggested to create a work order and have [facility maintenance] clean the sink which is not an acceptable solution to restore employee confidence and support [the company safety campaign.]  OSHA has set firm rules for these kind of bio hazard cleaning / removal / similar process and this act committed by maintenance team is clear violation and disregard to fellow employees well being.'
Narrative 2 - '[At the gate] water cooler sanitization station. Aircraft Maintenance group worked on [an aircraft] and according to the gate crew worked on sewer lines of lavatory on [the aircraft]. After completing their work they walked to the water station and washed the tools on drinking water cooler sanitization station. The incident was reported immediately to the Supervisor. It is very gross bio-hazard and unacceptable by any hygiene standard.

Approximately one hour after takeoff while performing routine oil level checks; discovered right engine oil to be low at 12 quarts (normal should be between approximately 16 and 19 quarts). Made satellite phone call to dispatch and maintenance control and agreed to return to ZZZZ.  Received ATC clearance to return to ZZZZ.  [Requested priority handling] and requested Airport Rescue and Firefighting.  Engine oil level continued to decrease and landed with 3 quarts remaining. Made normal overweight landing on runway XX. Shut down right engine after proper cooling time. Referenced brake cooling schedule. Taxied back to gate. Made all necessary logbook entries.Suggestion: Make sure routine oil level checks are made.

At approximately 4000 ft. on the arrival into ZZZ we received a call from the cabin stating that they had experienced a dirty sock smell in the aft cabin during the decent. The Flight Attendant 1 let us know that everyone was ok and the smell had dissipated. As we were already on vectors for the approach we continued to land and proceeded to the Gate without further incident. A logbook entry was made and an Odor incident form was completed. No odor was ever noticed in the Cockpit.

Student landed on Runway X at ZZZ with the intention of a full-stop landing. Landing was good; however; student burnt hand on his iPad (Hot from resting in the sunlight) and his reaction to it was to move his hand. His hand hit the throttle by mistake and caused an unintentional application of power and momentary loss of aircraft control leading to the aircraft momentarily veering off of the runway. The aircraft remained mostly on the runway. Student was able to regain control of the aircraft and taxi off of the runway safely. The student was okay and the aircraft undamaged after incident.

On the last leg after a four day trip; in VMC conditions; the Initial IFR Clearance stated 'Fly runway heading'. Pilot-Flying (FO) briefed terrain; obstacles avoidance by using ODP. Takeoff clearance given by ATC included 'Left turn direct ZZZZZ; traffic is in 2 miles final'. As a result; PF (Pilot Flying) executed a left turn at 500 ft. under VMC; verifying full obstacle clearance. During the initial climb the PF's radio altimeter was unreadable (reading changed rapidly) and uncorrelated with the Pilot-Monitoring (Captain)'s radio altimeter which showed solid climbing readings; and a single EGPWS alarm was noted (Whoop-Whoop; Pull Up); correspondingly both pilots verified again clearing of obstacles and terrain proximity. Later; during the approach to the destination; radio altimeter showed reading only on the PM (Pilot Monitoring) (Captain) side; which were uncorrelated with the current actual altitude. Traffic clearance concern: If takeoff clearance wouldn't include the word 'direct' but 'on course'; the correlation between the 2 miles on-final traffic to the left turn on course wouldn't be to expedite the turn by the Pilot Flying for traffic avoidance (also; in case of a Go-around by the landing plane). ATC clearance should be stated: 'Left turn on course ZZZZZ' / 'Left turn on course' would be sufficient for the Pilot Flying to execute his climb planning as planned during the preflight.

During taxi out for departure an aircraft reported to ATC that they saw a small one time flame from our number 2 engine. We were in direct view of ZZZ Control Tower and they indicated all looked normal. No other aircraft or our cabin crew saw any abnormalities. I opted to secure the engine and request an inspection by ARFF before returning to the gate. ARFF reported that there was no fire or evidence that one occurred and cleared us to continue. I returned to the gate for a normal passenger deplaning. Spoke with maintenance and made an AML entry. We were assigned another aircraft and preceded to depart for ZZZ1.

We were the first flight going into ZZZ with a storm in the area. The winds were gusting up to 47 knots with ATC getting weather updates real time that were a bit delayed in sharing that information with us. We had to divert to ZZZ1.Cause: There was a runway change due to a bad storm right over the field of ZZZ. We were setup for the ILS XX into ZZZ but they switched runways to do the ILS XY. Weather was being updated in real time so ATC could only give us the weather they had which was the ceilings being indefinite and the visibility at 2.5 miles. Winds were also reported at a gust of 47 knots slightly off the right. During the approach; we got a terrain warning when I disconnected the autopilot. I had a stable rate of descent and I could see the runway visually but shortly after; we got the red windshear alert. We did the escape maneuver that quickly went away so we configured for the normal go around profile. In the climb we were about 200 lbs over our bingo fuel so we diverted to the ZZZ1.Suggestion: Hold prior to the approach until weather is updated.'
Narrative 2 - 'A storm was moving from west to east. We were the first aircraft to arrive in ZZZ with the storm moving in. ATC didn't update ATIS although there were significant changes; including wind shifts and significant increases in velocity; resulting in a runway change from Runway XX to XY. Winds after finding out the runway change was 240 @ 20 gusting 47 at the peak. We were setup on the ILS XY; around 700 ft AGL GPWS terrain occurred. Shortly after around 400 ft AGL we received a red wind shear warning. Captain did the escape maneuver and made the decision to divert due to weather. We evaluated fuel and the weather and decided that was the safest course of action. We diverted to ZZZ1 and got in with no issue.Suggestion: Hold to attempt to wait out weather.

An electrical odor became viral in Main Cabin 5 minutes before door closure. Flight Attendant Y smelled a burn wiring odor in the cabin during boarding and after door closure. The Flight Deck was notified immediately on both occasions. However there wasn't notifications of a fire. Old or defective air vents tend to be the cause of burn wiring smell during the summer as the aircraft cools down. I immediately secured everything in the Galley and walk into the Cabin to inspect the situation with the intentions to fight an electrical fire. The aircraft returned to the Gate and deplaned following protocol. The Mechanics came on board at ZZZ Airport to inspect the aircraft for any bad wiring.
Missing sign for Taxiway J (no yellow sign with black 'J') indicating approaching J while taxiing south on A.

At XA29 on Day 0; I was acting as PM on a Flight from ZZZZ [airport] to ZZZ [airport]. We were making the left turn to park at a stand on the Southeast Ramp in ZZZ. The safety area was clear; a marshaller and wing walkers were in place; and the lead marshaller was actively marshalling us. All of a sudden; a tug violated the safety area from our left; entering the silhouette at a rapid rate of speed in front of our left wing; passing in front of our #1 engine; crossing in front of us on the lead-in line; and finally parking behind the air stairs. The lead marshaller signalled for us to stop; and the captain immediately applied braking to stop the aircraft; our nose offset approximately 45 degrees from the lead-in line at this point. The marshaller gestured at the tug driver to get out of the silhouette; to which the tug driver simply shrugged in response. As soon as the tug cleared the safety area; we resumed parking without incident. After speaking with ground personnel over the intercom (not the tug driver; but someone who claims to have spoken with them after the flight); we ascertained that the tug driver claimed to have seen the air stairs violating the safety area; and that was their reasoning for cutting us off during the parking process. However; the air stairs were not adjusted or otherwise moved after the tug cut us off; and only began to move once we had parked. I would like to emphasize that at the start of this event; we were entering the stand to park; we were actively being marshalled; and both myself and my captain had verified that the entire safety area was clear of any hazards to the aircraft; including the air stairs.Cause: The tug driver's decision to violate the safety area; whether intentionally or absent-mindedly; while we were in the process of parking the aircraft.Suggestions: Ground personnel training and overall situational awareness should both be increased to the point where these incidents never happen.

Flight was from ZZZ1 - ZZZ. Planned for 4.5 in route. Along the route moderate to severe turbulence was experienced which cased the continuation of the flight at 7;500 feet. The decent into ZZZ was accompanied by intermediate moderate turbulence. I was established on a stabilized approach into Runway XX at ZZZ. and was aware of possible wind shear and moderate turbulence reported. IAS was at 100 knots with 10deg of flaps on short final. Speed was adjusted higher to accommodate and was aiming for 1000 ft. markings. Floating and wind correcting was applied. About 10-20 feet above the surface wind shear was indicated and full power was applied. The aircraft drifted right and continue to sink rapidly. The aircraft struck the runway and continued to bounce as directional control was still NA. The aircraft left the right side of Runway XX striking a runway light on the right main gear. The aircraft continued to travel through the grass between Runway XX and the taxiway. The aircraft rejoined the pavement near taxiway 1 and taxiway 2 were the aircraft came to a halt. Runway XX was closed and I was escorted by fire rescue to the FBO. On visual inspection damage was seen to be only the wheel pants of the right pilot side main. Further inspection will be needed.

Directly after take off we had a full power loss between 20-50 feet AGL. We landed immediately; straight ahead on the runway; applied brakes and stopped the aircraft. No damage was done to A/C or runway surface. After landing; the a/c continued to run at idle.  While inspecting the aircraft to figure out the problem; the Instructor and I looked at the fuel selector and saw it was selected to the left tank. However; we had taken off with 'both' selected. We decided that; while moving the rudder pedals; my leg pushed the fuel selector in between the 'both' and 'left' detents; and bounced to 'left' on landing. For verification of the issue we taxied back and replicated the issue (with success or failure?). The fuel selector is the Dakota STC fuel selector PN DC11383. The Dakota fuel selector has a large handle that is easy to catch on a body or clothing and creates more leverage than needed. I believe the larger handle is safety issue that can cause fuel starvation in flight.

Aircraft X was flying IFR from ZZZ to LWB. Upon checking on frequency I informed the pilots of the altimeter; ATIS code; and the expected approach into LWB. At around XA02; I turned Aircraft X left as a vector for the approach and informed them of an icing report about 15 minutes prior near the airport. After clearing them direct to HODFU; an initial approach fix for the RNAV Runway 22; I informed Aircraft X of their position relative to the fix. They were given an crossing restriction of 065 or above HODFU and cleared for the approach at XA06. This altitude complies with the MIA in that area north of the airport. Aircraft X read back the instructions correctly. At XA07; I observed Aircraft X descend to 062. I informed him to check his altitude and that he was 300 feet low. I repeated the crossing restriction. Aircraft X responded similar to 'Aircraft X Six thousand five hundred. Got it.'. Aircraft X descended to 052 before climbing back up to 065 then continuing the approach after HODFU. Recommendation: Any pilots unfamiliar with the airport or procedures should ask questions and pay close attention to detail when flying into airports near mountains. The approach chart also shows the bottom altitude for HODFU is lower than our MIA at the center level. I think this causes confusion with some pilots as they expect lower at HODFU than they are given and could lead to mistakes being made.

Aircraft departed ZZZ1 at XA:32 intending for a dual local flight. No abnormalities were detected in preflight or run-up. Oil quantity was at 6 quarts and warm. In cruise flight at 4500 FT; the engine began to experience a partial power loss. Engine started choking and going in and out and we felt overall roughness and saw RPMs dropping then rising then repeating rapidly. Disconnected autopilot and turned towards ZZZ airport to divert. IP (Flight Instructor) ran memory items and SP (Student Pilot) ran engine checklist to troubleshoot for engine failure and followed QRH for partial power loss. Engine was still experiencing the same abnormalities. Called airport traffic and announced we were inbound for a landing. Power was idle at this point and we were fully gliding down to land. Runway XX was in use and there were multiple aircraft in the pattern. Aircraft was lined up too high on runway XX so IP circled to land runway XY and executed a power off 180 to land on the runway. Aircraft touched down at ZZZ at XA:58. The aircraft had enough momentum to taxi us off the runway and onto the ramp. IP called dispatch for help and rescue from ZZZ. We were not asked if we were ok or if we needed anything; and in fact we were asked if the aircraft was damaged first as that was the main concern. My student and I's well being and safety did not seem of concern to management and we were treated as an afterthought. We were told someone was to come get us via plane asap; however; IP discovered this flight was intending to complete an entire dual lesson then come get us at the very end. We were told they were en route and were going to come get us after 'a few touch and goes as to not have to incomplete the lesson'. This was discovered to not be truthful and once pressed on the matter; an individual came to get us via car. Only after contacting a third individual who is an ACP (Assistant Chief Pilot); was there any urgency for our situation and care for IP and SP.

My instructor and I were doing touch and goes at FLY in Aircraft X. Throughout our time there we made the proper radio calls for an uncontrolled airfield. On our third and final lap at FLY we were departing the area on the upwind from Runway 33 and were notified of ADSB traffic in very close proximity. The ADSB traffic in question was Aircraft Y. The pilot of the Aircraft Y not only did not provide enough spacing; but did not make their proper radio calls and ignored our radio calls. After we were notified of the ADSB traffic; we proceeded to ask Aircraft Y of their intentions and if they had us in sight. They ignored both my radio call and my instructors. Since they were at our 6 o'clock; we did not see the traffic until they were turning crosswind off our right wing (and flying faster than us). In short; the Aircraft Y pilot was not following uncontrolled airport etiquette and came dangerously close without acknowledging us.

Media reports on Day 0 'Four unusual aircraft have been shot down by U.S. fighter jets over North America this month...and ignited debate over the safety of the continent's skies.'  A picture was taken last week from a golf course near ZZZ.  It clearly shows the 'Chinese Spy Balloon' and a commercial airliner flying beneath it.  As a Captain responsible for the safety of my passengers and crew; I am concerned about these recent incidents.  Recent company communications and pilot notices contain no information on any of these events.  Do these objects pose a significant flight safety risk?  What is being done to mitigate this risk?I realize this is a new problem; and we won't have all the answers to every question I propose.  But please tell us what level of risk these objects pose to our flying operations; and what measures are being done to mitigate this risk.

I was not present on the flight deck during this event. It was relayed to me immediately after completion of the appropriate checklist completion.Left engine generator fault light and left engine generator drive light came on simultaneously. Left engine drive fault checklist was accomplished. APU started per checklist and was operating normally. No other faults or abnormal operating parameters were observed. Maintenance Control was contacted. All parties agreed it was ok to continue. ACARS maintenance discrepancy was entered into logbook.On touchdown at ZZZ the APU fault light came on and the APU shut down. After clearing the runway the APU fault checklist was accomplished. APU was successfully restarted. Taxied to the gate.Aircraft maintenance personnel greeted the crew in the jetway and stated it looked like significant damage had been caused by the IDG (Integrated Drive Generator) coming apart inside the engine compartment.

We were filed for the Jackson 1 Departure to intercept V122 to BRUTT intersection. With LNAV and VNAV engaged on departure; the SID cannot be executed properly due to the language written on the SID. On departure; we turned prematurely before OED VOR; which the SID specifically states you must cross directly over.We were queried by ATC about not crossing directly over the VOR; and asked to call Cascade Approach on landing. I spoke with the Supervisor; and he stated that this has been an ongoing problem with this departure. I offered to write the report to raise awareness for our pilot group to prevent a possible pilot deviation.

Before taxiing out of the FBO; ground gave incorrect taxi instruction until prompted a second time of our location. Crossed XXL & XXR separately on Taxiway 1 without incident. After receiving takeoff clearance to depart XY; we commenced our static; flaps 2 departure for decreased runway takeoff distance and released brakes. At approximately 50 to 60 knots we noticed a Moony aircraft taxiing on Taxiway 2 from the north to south of the field crossing XY; and that they weren't stopping. After aborting takeoff we proceeded to wait the SOP criteria time for brake cooling and departed for ZZZ. Suggestions: Ground and tower were not communicating.'
Narrative 2 - 'We were cleared takeoff by ZZZ Tower and performed all SOPs. IT was a static takeoff because of the limited takeoff distance. I released brakes and began the takeoff roll normally. At about 50 KIAS we noticed a Mooney taxiing right to left on Taxiway 1 and not slowing down to hold short of our takeoff runway. The Mooney continued to cross our takeoff path and we aborted the takeoff; per our SOPs prior to the Mooney being clear of our takeoff path. Informed ZZZ Tower of the abort and taxied clear of Runway XX. Cooled brakes in accordance with SOPs and departed without further incident.Suggestions: ZZZ Ground Control and Tower were not communicating well with aircraft or with each other even though the airport was not busy due to Runway XYR/XAL being closed; which excluded most of the larger aircraft.

I was landing behind Aircraft Y. They had landed about 3 minutes before me. At 60 feet AGL I hit their wake vortex.  My aircraft rolled hard to the left; maxing out at about a 25 degree bank which required a significant aileron deflection to correct.  I would estimate aileron deflection was approximately 80-90% of what was available.  I quickly stabilized the aircraft and continued to a normal landing.

While taxing on ramp we were parked with the parking brake set while waiting for our parking spot to become available. We received an ECAM fault yellow hydraulic system low pressure followed by a complete loss of yellow hydraulics. I noticed the aircraft started to move on its own. In an attempt to stop the moving aircraft I and my First Officer (FO) applied full brake pressure to the toe brakes and selected all brake settings in an attempt to stop the aircraft. The aircraft continued to move. My FO suggested using thrust reverse. So in the heat of the moment I applied reverse thrust. The aircraft stopped moving. Maintenance approached the aircraft to chock the nose gear which allowed us to safely shut down the engines. The aircraft was then towed to parking. We were informed by Maintenance that a hydraulic hose had failed over the right main gear brakes.'
Narrative 2 - 'After taxiing into the ramp we had to wait behind an MD-11 that was in the process of being towed into park. The Captain set the parking brake until we were cleared into our parking spot. After the taxi route was clear; but before cleared to taxi to our spot; we received a Yellow Hydraulic pressure low indication on the ECAM and the aircraft started to move forward. The Captain then attempted to stop the aircraft using all brake settings. I heard him exclaim we have no brakes as the aircraft began to slowly move forward. I attempted my toe brakes as well and all brake settings but nothing was stopping the aircraft. I called on ramp multiple times informing them of the situation and our need for assistance. I suggested to try reverse thrust which worked in stopping the aircraft. We were able to get the aircraft chalked; shutdown the engines; and towed into parking. After engine shutdown we were informed by Maintenance that the a hydraulic hose had failed over the right main gear brakes.

The flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 was the third leg of our day. We had landed at XA00Z which was an hour advance of planned passenger's arrival. Our passengers soon notified us of late arrival upon which I checked to ensure we would not be affected by EDCT (Estimated Departure Time Clearance) and that weather wouldn't be a factor. I then obtained our flight clearance which included a full route meaning we weren't getting our shorter overwater route. That route would also avoid any of the approaching weather by a wide margin. I re-ran our flight plan to ensure we had adequate fuel as the new one was 110 NM longer and would slightly change winds. The original route required 3;570 lbs total including enroute burn; 45 min reserve; and alternate based on cruise altitude of FL400. No alternate was required though as destination weather was > 5000/5 for the entire day and projected to remain so. Still; we plan and carry alternate fuel anytime we have the ability to do so. I had rounded the final fuel load up to 4;000 lbs total as it's all too common flying in or out of ZZZ3 airspace and suddenly getting significantly different routing or held down below cruise altitude for a bit. That decision would prove critical in preventing a divert later in flight. We boarded passengers at XB30Z and were given taxi clearance to 30. Upon nearing the runway; we were told to taxi to the holding area and would start taxi again at XB50Z for a XB54Z release. Approaching XC00Z; we were cleared to taxi and then into position and hold where we sat for approximately 3 minutes before being cleared for takeoff. Shortly after checking in with departure; we were given a 250 kt speed restriction and then given multiple vectors 90 degrees off of route. During most of this we were held below 15;000 ft. After being cleared back onto our flight plan; we were step climbed 6 times until we reached FL 330 about 30 minutes into the flight. During this time we also had to request deviations for weather. A slight left deviation would've allowed us to safely clear all the weather even at the lower altitude; but all aircraft were being directed that right was the only choice. Based on what traffic we had directly in view and on TCAS; it didn't make sense as it looked clear with all possible conflicts being to the west. We attempted to work right but even with significant deviations directly westward we were going to be boxed in by cells. Both NEXRAD and our onboard radar indicated yellow to red echoes well above our current altitude. We and other aircraft at higher altitudes continued to request eastward deviations and were denied. We also repeatedly requested higher as that would've been a satisfactory way of being able to comply with what they needed; but again were denied. At this point; I told the ZZZ3 Center controller that we had no choice but to go left as there was no place we could safely penetrate the weather. They finally relented and after a short deviation that was within 2-3 NM east of the course line; we were around it and back on flight plan. I was prepared to declare pilot authority to deviate for safety of aircraft; passengers and crew had they not. Between the additional ground time; ATC vectors; deviations; and hold down; we had eaten significantly into the additional fuel and were showing below a 45 min reserve if we remained at the lower altitude. This was even after seeing the deteriorating fuel state early and slowing down significantly from cruise speed to M.65. After again requesting further climb and being denied; I declared minimum fuel. Instead of the controller acknowledging; we were shifted to the next controller. Upon checking in; we were still held down and told to expect some time before climb. I again interjected on the radio that we were minimum fuel which was acknowledged by the new controller by him stating; 'uh..ah...well; ok.' He then stated we wouldn't get any further climb until with ZZZ4 Center. By that time we would be over State andstill at FL330 just over an hour into flight. The PM and I evaluated the fuel state and knowing the potential ATC delays we could face in ZZZ1 area airspace despite the great weather that we may be facing a divert. I kept our home base of ZZZ5 and ZZZ6 in mind should that be required. We set 1;000 lbs as an acceptable; safe fuel state needed to both put us above minimum fuel and give us some additional in the event of further delays. After ensuring ZZZ4 Center knew of our fuel state; we were held down for nearly another 10 minutes and then stepped 4 times from FL330 to FL400. After reaching FL400; we pulled back to M.67 and finally saw 1;100 lbs overhead destination and decided to continue. I considered requesting FL430; but based on less tailwind and the increased burn to climb I decided it wouldn't be beneficial. Fuel state improved to 1;280 lbs as the winds shifted and thanks to a small shortcut by Center. During decent with ZZZ4 Center; we were turned roughly 120 degrees off the arrival and it wasn't until questioning the controller if he knew that we had declared that he stated no and turned us back towards ZZZ1. Even though I had never rescinded the previous declaration; it apparently had not been passed to some of the subsequent ATC sectors. I told the controller that we were currently above min fuel but would not continue to be with continued vectors away from destination. We were shortly passed off to the approach controller and landed uneventfully from the RNAV XX. Final fuel state at shutdown was 1;145 lbs.Our passengers being on time might have alleviated some of this as weather had not moved onto our route at that time. More fuel would've have also created more pad; but the additional alternate fuel that wasn't required by regulation or the situation plus additional contingency fuel should've been more than sufficient to prevent it. Getting held down well below planned cruise altitude until almost halfway through a 2.5hr flight is pretty uncommon but played the biggest role in this.

Inbound to FXE on the FISEL SEVEN ARRIVAL. We were given a vector off of the arrival track and cleared to 3000 ft. Several miles Northwest of FXE on approximately a left downwind for the approach to Runway 09; as we were approaching level off at 3000 ft. we received a 'Traffic' warning from TCAS. Target was noted on the display at about 10 o'clock less than 1000 ft. below our altitude and well within the 3 mile circle; with a climbing indication (up arrow). As we continued on assigned heading at 3000 ft. the target appeared to be closing on our track and continuing to climb. Shortly after level off the TCAS issued a 'Climb' command. At this point I noted that the target was indicating 300 ft. below our altitude. I initiated the climb and called for the PM (Pilot Monitoring) to advise ATC of TCAS CLIMB. ATC acknowledged by calling out VFR traffic to us and stating that it was 'never above 2000 ft.' I acquired the target visually (low wing piston single) and observed it to be converging with our track from the left and close to our altitude. It is difficult to judge distance in this context; but we routinely pass aircraft that are 1000 ft. above/below our altitude. In my judgement the target in this case was much closer. We reached about 3600 ft. before TCAS went to a neutral vertical speed command; and the target aircraft was still indicating less than 1000 ft. below. By this time target was behind our aircraft and distance was increasing. Shortly after that TCAS issued a 'Clear of Conflict' and we returned to 3000 ft. The rest of the flight was uneventful; except to note that the same controller put us on a vector for the left base and then sent us beyond the final for Runway 09 while dealing with multiple VFR aircraft.

On descent into ZZZ; I was the pilot monitoring; on the way we were cleared from 17;000 ft to 5;300 ft to commence our approach into ZZZ. Leaving 16;000 the plane experienced a loss of oil pressure in our #2 engine. After taking a few moments to assess the situation I had confirmed the warning message with the supporting oil pressure gauge on ED1 as it read 7 psi. From there I handed the radios over to the Captain as I proceeded to the appropriate QRH procedure for R ENG OIL PRESS. Following the steps of this procedure very carefully; I was led to shut down our #2 engine in flight through the In-flight engine shut down procedure. After which I then completed the single engine approach and landing procedure. During this time the Captain; flew and maintained control of the aircraft; alerted ATC; as well as alerting the flight attendant of the situation. We landed safely in ZZZ where we were cleared by ARFF and taxied to the gate.

I was flying into [the] Seaplane base in ZZZ on the VFR Arrival procedure at 1200 MSL.  After contacting the tower and being assigned the route arrival procedure the tower called out traffic for me 1 o'clock altitude unknown.  I told the tower I was searching for the traffic.  The tower told the conflict aircraft my position and they called me insight.  As I continued to search for the traffic an aircraft appeared at my 12 o'clock at extremely close range and my altitude head on.  I had little to no time to react but attempted to push forward and descend and avoid a collision.My aircraft and the conflict traffic collided head on approximately 5 nm north of ZZZ just South of the reporting point [landmark].  My aircraft continued to be controllable and I slowed the aircraft to reduce the risk of structural failure.  I could not see any obvious damage from the cockpit but had heard and felt the impact.  I told the tower I believed I have had a mid air collision and requested the tower to ask the other aircraft if they we OK.  I don't know if anyone responded to the tower.  I continued into ZZZ and landed in the water lane without further incident.  Upon parking the aircraft in the float slip I inspected the aircraft and found minor damage to the right hand fiberglass wingtip from the collision.  No other damage has been discovered at this point.I called the tower on my cell phone and told them I had made contact with the other aircraft.  I then called the FAA and reported the mid air collision.  My aircraft is ADS-B equipped but I believe the other aircraft was not.  I never received any warning on my traffic display and I know it was working from other aircraft warnings on the same flight earlier.  I still do not know the identity of the other aircraft.The area of the [landmark] north of ZZZ is a high traffic area and possible collision risk.  I have operated out of ZZZ for XX plus years without incident.  I believe if the other aircraft had ADS-B and or mode C we could have avoided the collision.  I don't know what could have been done better with the exception of ADS-B on the other aircraft and honestly feel lucky to be alive.

On climb out with the autopilot engaged; I noticed a slight pitch down on several occasions. We were in light chop so I wasn't overly concerned. Once at cruise altitude in smooth air; I felt a slight bump and noticed the vertical speed show approximately 600-700 FPM descent. The autopilot immediately arrested the decent and maintained altitude. No ECAM message was received. A few minutes later it reoccurred. A minor thump followed by a momentary pitch down. This continued several times and seemed to be increasing but only slightly. Considering the aircraft had been written up the previous flight for 'F/CTL ELEV SERVO FAULT DISPLAYED IN FLIGHT LEFT ELEV GREEN HYD SYSTEM '  and signed off with 'RESET ELAC 1 AND 2 OPS CK GOOD' we were concerned about possibility of the situation becoming worse and decided to divert to ZZZ. I slowed the aircraft to see if that would somehow resolve the issue to no avail. The aircraft continued with the thump and pitch issues at least 15 times during the flight.  We landed in ZZZ safely. Captain contacted maintenance and tracking. We received a call and we were treated very well and professionally.Cause - Possibly a quick sign off on the previous flightSuggestion - Possibly more follow up on write ups especially flight control issues

The lights that illuminate the sidewalk behind the gates in RDU make it nearly impossible to see ramp markings or anything else while approaching the gate area at night in the rain. Luckily the Marshaller must have known this because he stood on the yellow lead in line and emphatically and consistently motioned with his lighted wands to where the lead in line was until we were about 10ft from the stopping point. Poor design in ramp lighting.Suggestion: Some sort of cover on the lights that allows the lights to shine down on the sidewalk; but not straight out to approaching aircraft.

We were Filed and Cleared for 'RNDRZ1 Arrival ILS 26L' in LAS. We set and Descended to 8;000 ft. with Managed Descend Mode. Controller then gave us Descend to 6;000 ft. and pointed out traffic. When we leveled off at 6;000 feet; I queried the controller by transmitting Level 6;000 ft. just passing BERBN Fix. He said 'Roger' as we continued to look for our traffic. We were coupled with ILS 26L and the aircraft started to turn after HOGOG Fix to Heading 020. It is only then; the Controller gave us vector to 080 even as he pointed out the traffic. He then told us that we should have picked up 080 heading after BERBN. RNDRZ1 states at BERBN FIX that 'Landing RWY19L/R; 26L/R EXPECT RADAR vectors to final approach course'. Controller never gave us a vector after BERBN and since Aircraft X Connects from BERBN-BISHP-HOGOG-KODSE-HUXAR; AC started the turn to 020.The initial clearance from ATC was too close to Descend Via Cleared for the ILS 26L. Traffic watch was involved. On the Arrival (which is New) the INSET does NOT display a Track of 079 only a small print that says 079 track after BERBN. This is Aircraft X specific when we select the STAR and APPROACH. I suggest that ATC proactively assign a heading prior to or after BERBN just as they to in LAX after SLI Heading 340 on GOATZ1 Arrival. Train Crews to clear the Waypoint after BERBN so there is a Discontinuity which would Default to 079 Heading.'
Narrative 2 - 'We were filed and cleared for the RNDRZ1 arrival ILS 26L. I set 8;000 ft. in managed descent. Controller then cleared us to 6;000 feet and pointed out traffic. Leveled off at 6;000 feet and the Captain informed ATC that we were at 6;000 feet and passing BERBN and response was Roger. Continued to actively look for traffic. I was coupled to ILS 26L and just as the aircraft at HOGOG started it's turn the Controller gave us a 080 heading and was pointing out traffic at the same time. Then the controller stated that we should have flown a 080 heading out of BERBN. The RNDRZ1 states at BERBN fix that landing runway 26L expect radar vectors.From ATC initial clearance is too close to descend VIA for ILS 26L. Traffic watch was involved. Arrival the INSET does not display a track of 079 after BERBN only in the small print does it show 079. ATC should issue a heading at BERBN. The aircraft did not to link to the approach or to the arrival or remove the linked portion.

I was practicing air taxiing and quick stops with a 31-hour student pilot on a taxiway. During the recovery phase of the quick stop; the student did not raise enough collective to arrest the descent. I took controls at around 30 feet AGL and increased the collective to our 5-minute limit; but we continued to descend and impacted the ground hard enough to spread the skids. A piece of non-structural sheet metal detached from the underside of the helicopter and landed beside the taxiway. I reported what happened to the tower and they sent someone to retrieve the sheet metal. I flew the helicopter back to the flight school's ramp and did not observe any damage other than the spread skids. I should have taken the controls earlier and not allowed the descent rate to develop to an unrecoverable state. I was trying to talk the student through the correct control inputs when I should have just abandoned the maneuver and recovered.

Sitting on the ramp in ZZZ where a power out is required. We were advised we were clear to start engine 2 then 1. We started both engines normally and Captain called for slats extend after start checklist. I moved the handle to slats extend and when looking up to continue my flow on the overhead panel; it appeared that we were slightly moving. Due to it being dark and with zero lights on the ramp it was very hard to tell and asked aloud; are we moving? Once I gathered my attention solely to the movement I recognized we were slowly moving forward and pressed the brakes fully right as the Captain set the parking brake. He immediately radioed down to make sure everyone was okay. Once we gathered ourselves he realized that we had forgotten to run the preflight checklist; which confirms that the parking brake is set. This was yet another reminder on the importance of checklist usage and how both pilots need to remain vigilant on accomplishing these required tasks.'
Narrative 2 - 'We received the weight and balance numbers fairly early in the loading process so we loaded and confirmed them. I did my take off briefing after which I usually call for the preflight checklist. However because we weren't anywhere near done loading I decided to wait for the checklist breaking my established habit pattern. After loading was complete we ran the before start checklist and started engines. During the second engine start my First Officer noticed we were moving and I put on the brakes. I didn't hear anything from ground but saw him running off the nose. We sat there for a couple minutes trying to figure out what happened and thought ground might reconnect. But it was obvious he was not coming back to the airplane and the Marshal was signaling to taxi out so we did. We called into operations on taxi to check and make sure everyone was safe. They said everyone was fine so we departed. Not adhering to established habit patterns and failing to run the preflight checklist could have injured a good man in ZZZ. I'll stick to what I always do so this doesn't happen again.

On climbout the electric trim failed to operate on either side.  Evaluated the situation to determine the appropriate checklist. Requested priority handling; notified company; advised flight attendants; planned for a flap 15 landing per the checklist and had Fire/Rescue standing by.  Later the Speed Trim Fail light illuminated intermittently.  Due to time; WX and familiarity with ZZZ; ZZZ1 and ZZZ2; we made the decision to continuing to ZZZ2 (VFR; long runways; low traffic demand and distance to each)'
Narrative 2 - 'Upon takeoff from ZZZ the FO (PF) side electric trim was unresponsive.  The CA then attempted electric trim with also no response.  Priority handling was requested; the non-normal checklist was completed; the FO hand flew the aircraft to ZZZ2 as filed with an uneventful approach and landing.  Crash and fire rescue teams were requested and followed the aircraft to the gate for an uneventful shut down.

Briefed rejected takeoff criteria and actions prior to push. Normal pushback and taxi. Maintenance had requested a TOGA takeoff. On the takeoff roll; PF (FO) advanced levers to spool the engines to approximately 1.05 EPR (Engine Pressure Ratio). Once reached; levers were advanced to TOGA. While not hearing 80 knots; I (PF) glanced at instruments; noticed that the needle of #1 EPR was not set and the engine was not producing the power it should have been. The CA was diagnosing this at the 80 knots callout and called and executed a rejected takeoff. The aircraft speed at time of reject was between approximately 80 and 100 knots. I notified ATC of the reject and we stopped and turned off the runway normally. The CA announced remain seated and we reviewed the aircraft systems; brake temperatures and saw that everything was indicating normal. We notified ATC we did not require assistance; coordinated with local tech ops; and operations for a return to the gate and taxied in normally. Observations from the CA.Arriving at the dark aircraft; upon selecting ground power I found the APU master switch on and an APU Emergency Shutdown ECAM present. MX (Maintenance) was called to perform a reset. The logbook had been left with past pages hidden behind the flap and no current clean page established; and as the power up checklist was completed; the parking brake was discovered in the OFF position. The fact that the aircraft was in disarray for no apparent reason resulted in a heightened expectation of additional hidden threats. I completed the walk around and everything appeared normal. As the ground crew prepared for pushback with doors closed and the jetbridge pulled; they advised of a cut and chord showing on the #1 main tire. MX had determined a tire change was required. The chock had blocked the tire damage from being observed. All these minor issues led to an uneasy feeling of the hair standing up on the back of my neck; and may have helped set the tone in the reject. The logbook had a request for a TOGA takeoff and we briefed that as well. Initial power application was normal; acceleration appeared normal; engine indications appeared normal at first run through. Approaching 80 kts as I scanned back through the engine gauges and prepared to announce '80 kts power set' the number 1 EPR was clearly not at the target position. It took a second to verify that it wasn't a fluctuation and was relatively steady state. There was not enough time to assess well; how much power was actually being produced; but I could not honestly make the call 'power set' either. The fact that we still had almost 70 kts of additional acceleration to accomplish and not knowing if the power was adequate or would remain adequate for the rest of the takeoff role; led to the decision to discontinue the takeoff. Because we had crossed into the high speed regime and the internal company focus on that point; I believe; actually led to a delay in initiating the reject as it was another consequential gate in addition to V1 and the malfunction to consider the ramifications of. Ultimately; and as quickly as possible; I announced reject knowing we had more than adequate runway to stop. The deceleration rate was such that I unintentionally did not select idle reverse as my focus shifted from stopping; to not coming to a complete stop with the autobrakes. I should have unlocked the reversers regardless.

After leveling off at FL 320; Aircraft experienced at least 4 audible bangs and yawed. ECAM indication ENG1 STALL appeared twice and disappeared. Flight was inside of 80 miles from ZZZ. Crew [requested priority] and proceeded directly to ZZZ. All applicable checklists were executed. All required notifications were completed. ATC provided vectors to Runway XL at ZZZ. Aircraft cleared runway and was inspected by Airport Rescue and Firefighting before taxiing into the gate. Engine continued to run throughout the evolution.Compressor Stalls caused the crew to divert and land before a potential pending engine failure. Pilots need to maintain situational awareness and always have a plan for where to go in the event of a [failure].

At XA:30z time; my student and I performed a touch and go at ZZZ on the North runway; on initial climb out we decided the airspace was too congested for training and asked ZZZ Tower for a departure back to ZZZ1. Tower approved us to make a straight out departure to ZZZ1 and Frequency change was approved. My student bugged runway heading and we started our climb to 3;500 ft. MSL. While getting ZZZ1 ATIS; we observed a pair of V tail airplanes in formation on their climb out of the South runway approximately 100 ft. below our altitude(3;000-3;200 ft. at the time). I kept my eye on the traffic during our climb and while passing over [a road] I observed the flight of two making a left turn to the north that intercepted our flight path. I took controls from my student and immediately started a full power climb to 3;500 ft. MSL to avoid conflict. The flight passed underneath us at less than 500 ft. After we were clear of the aircraft and level at 3;500 ft. MSL and exiting the airspace still on our assigned straight out departure I contacted ZZZ Tower again to ask where; if any miscommunication had taken place. ZZZ Tower informed me that both myself and the formation flight were cleared for straight out departures and they had no authority over where they turn once they are outside their airspace. I said thank you and left the frequency again as to not cause any conflict; however where the flight of two had turned was about 1 mile inside of the ZZZ airspace where ZZZ Tower had approved both to make a straight out departure. I believe the factor that caused this situation was the flight of two aircraft that turned on course before exiting the airspace when being cleared straight out.

While approaching the weather from the east; we could see the weather which appeared to be non-threatening and only rain. Radar was painting light-moderate rain with a very small section of heavy. The heavy band appeared to only be 1-2 miles wide. As we navigated; making small deviation to the left; we experienced a flash and heard a loud boom.
